parts:
On Mon, 2012-08-20 at 10:50 -0700, Alexander van Loon wrote:
> Hello,
>
> I just started using ggplot2 today. Starting was not easy due to the
> syntax being quite different from the default syntax of R (took me a
> while to figure out I had to use + signs), but ggplot2 does a much
> better job than R's basic functionality. I'd like to thank mr. Wickham
> and any other contributors for their work.
>
> I made some scatter plots which use stat_sum [1] to display sums of
> observations. Please use the script and the data I attached to see how
> this doesn't work completely as would be expected. The data only
> contains round numbers with no decimals. The plot
> scatterAPPRES_ggplot2.png is drawn correctly and you see the whole
> numbers from one to five in the legend. However, for the scatter plots
> for BSPRES, FPRSSR and FRAGHA stat_sum decides to use non round
> numbers with decimals (1.5 and so on). Is there something which can be
> done about this? The page for stat_sum [1] doesn't give any options to
> change the behavior, nor that I find anything else which could help
> with search engines.
>
> I also observe that the scaling of the dots can be too aggressive. In
> the APPRES scatter plot for example, the dot for five observations
> seems at least ten times larger than the dot for one observation
> instead of five times larger.
>
> Slightly off-topic, but I also have a second issue. You can see in the
> script that the line "scale_x_continuous("Inhabitants in thousands")
> +" is commented out for the scatter plot of INHABT. Actually I don't
> want to have it commented because I want the x axis to be renamed like
> that, but if I uncomment it the previous line with xlim gets ignored
> (while the x axis does get renamed then). Strange behavior. Doing the
> same thing in vanilla R also gave me trouble [2], but I managed to get
> it fixed. But for ggplot2 the syntax is different... if anyone could
> help me with this problem as well, I'd be delighted.
>
> Greetings,
> Alexander van Loon
>
> [1] http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/stat_sum.html
> [2]
> http://stackoverflow.com/questions/11728799/abline-and-logarithmic-x-axis-gives-horizontal-regression-line-in-plot/

Never mind the last issue, I read [1] and learned that it is a 'feature'
for scale_x_continuous to ignore any xlim command. I corrected it to the
following code:

scale_x_continuous("Inhabitants in thousands", limits=c(0,215))

[1] http://wiki.stdout.org/rcookbook/Graphs/Axes%20%28ggplot2%
29/#setting-range-and-reversing-direction-of-an-axis

messages.author: 5a37f1244321fb07
messages.subject: RE: stat_sum uses numbers with decimals, but data only has rounded numbers
parts:
Hi Alexander,
I don't know the answer for the "stat_sum" issue, but I think I know why "scale_x_continuous" behaves like this.


In your original code:

...
xlim(0, 215) +
scale_x_continuous("Inhabitants in thousands") +

...

The default setting for limits is "NULL" for scale_x_continuous, so x-limits are overwritten (to NULL) even you specify it before.

Therefore, if you switch the order as:
scale_x_continuous("Inhabitants in thousands") +

xlim(0, 215) +
...

...then, it will work.

Or, you can specify the limits within scale_x_continuous:

scale_x_continuous("Inhabitants in thousands", limits=c(0,215)) +

Hope this helps...
Kaori

messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: Re: stat_sum uses numbers with decimals, but data only has rounded numbers
parts:
A few things about this:

- It makes it much easier to see and diagnose problems if a simple
reproducible example is used. See the link at the bottom of these
mailing list messages for how to do this. If readers of the mailing
list can simply copy and paste the code, then they are much more
likely to help.

- Presently the 'size' parameter is scaled so that the range of the
data is mapped (linearly) to the radius range 1 to 6. This means there
are two hurdles in making a balloon plot, where the area is
proportional to the value.
First, since the data range is mapped to the size/radius range, this
means that if your data goes from 1-6, those values get mapped to the
same size range as if the data goes from 20-40. The smallest data
values get mapped to size 1, and the largest data values get mapped to
size 6. This may seem counterintuitive, but it is the same way that
mappings work for, say, color gradients: the smallest data value is
mapped to the color on one end of the gradient, and the largest data
value is mapped to the color on the other end, no matter what the data
values are. This can be addressed by setting the limits and range for
the scale.
Second, since the values are mapped linearly with respect to radius,
even if you fix the first issue, there's still a problem. Suppose, for
convenience, that your data goes from 1-6. Then a data value of 6 will
be represented by a circle that's twice the radius for a data value of
3 -- meaning it will be 4x the area. Using scale_area will address
this issue.

- The presence of the decimal points in the legend is not necessarily
a bug. stat_sum calculates numeric values. Even though the values for
that particular stat are always integers, to the rest of ggplot2, they
are simply values on a continuous (as opposed to discrete) scale. It
uses the same break-calculation algorithm as it does for any other
continuous values, and the result is that if the range is 1-4, it
generates a legend that includes 0.5 steps. In other words, the
generality of ggplot2 involves some trade-offs - you get more
flexibility, but it may not be as good for every particular case. At
any rate, the way to make it not display decimal points is to use
something like breaks=1:4 in the scale.


-Winston

messages.author: f6a50671dfa0ce19
messages.subject: Re: stat_sum uses numbers with decimals, but data only has rounded numbers
parts:
Thank you very much for your reply Winston. Your advice to use the breaks option isn't entirely clear to me though. As you recommend, a minimal example is the following:

data set is: http://alexandervanloon.nl/survey_oss.csv

code from the script to produce one of the scatter plots is:

# plot for boundary spanner presence
png("scatterBSPRES.png")
ggplot(survey, aes(x=BSPRES, y=OSSADP)) +
scale_x_continuous("Presence of boundary spanners") +
scale_y_continuous("Adoption of OSS") +
stat_sum(aes(size=..n..)) +
scale_area(range = c(1, 3)) +
geom_smooth(method=lm, se=FALSE)
dev.off()

and similarly:

# plot for fiscal pressure on ICT-department
png("scatterFPRSSR.png")
ggplot(survey, aes(x=FPRSSR, y=OSSADP)) +
scale_x_continuous("Fiscal pressure on ICT department") +
scale_y_continuous("Adoption of OSS") +
stat_sum(aes(size=..n..)) +
scale_area(range = c(1, 3)) +
geom_smooth(method=lm, se=FALSE)
dev.off()

This gives me two scatterplots which have legends displaying n from 1 to 4 in steps of 0.5. You mention I could add something like breaks=1:4 in the scale to solve it, but I don't understand;  adding them to either the x or y scale wouldn't work because I don't want to affect those breaks, only the breaks of stat_sum. But placing the breaks option in the stat_sum line like stat_sum(aes(size=..n..), breaks=1:4) + doesn't work. Could you please clarify?

Adding scale_area did work nicely for me, exactly what I needed.
